text.overview: P1: get over the moat that forms seasonally, scramble onto the ledge at the base, and pass two bolts to a single-bolt rappel station. P2: steep snow early in the season, or a few rock steps, then bear left along the ledge to a slung block, 30 meters along, that gives an optional stop (replace the tat if doubtful). P3: 30 meters further the ledge dead-ends in a small alcove; leftward a horizontal crack accepts cams for an anchor. With a 60m rope P2 and P3 link. Two exits above: skirt the alcove o

An alternative first pitch from the ledge at the base. The right-hand line is full trad and more likely to be dry, with a bolt near the bottom that can serve as a belay bolt. The left line (variation 1) has three high bolts, and early-season snowmelt may run down it. The second and third pitches and the descent match variation 1.

text.approach: Drive to the Sunrise Mine trailhead (Mountain Loop Highway, Forest Road 4065) and start up the Sunrise Mine Trail. Follow it about 2.5 miles, gaining to roughly 4,300 ft, to the last major switchback before the trail begins its final zigzag up toward Headlee Pass — this is the turnoff point, not the pass itself. Leave the maintained trail here and pick up a cairned traverse heading northeast across open talus toward Vega North Tower (also called Eros Tower). The line of cairns crosses two separate talus fields separated by strips of subalpine trees, passing a little above a large flat-topped boulder, which sits near the first stand of trees. This talus traverse is the shared approach for Mile High Club, Marvin's Ear, and Beyond Redlining, so cairns and a boot path are well established in season, but talus can be loose and slow going with a pack. A reliable fresh-water seep is at a red-rock outcrop in the Mile High gully, roughly at the base of the formation — worth topping off here since there's no water higher on the wall. Beyond Redlining's start is on the dark gray face directly above the two largest boulders at the base of the tower, just left of (west of) Mile High Club's start. Expect lingering steep snow against the base in early season, which can make the last stretch of the talus approach and the transition onto rock its own small crux.

text.overview: Beyond Redlining climbs the West Face of Vega North Tower (Eros Tower) in 11 sustained pitches (1,200 ft, Grade IV 5.10+; 8 of 11 pitches are 5.10 or harder), and finishing on the summit that Mile High Club also reaches. Established by Rad Roberts and Kurt Hicks in July 2020, it is a full grade harder, longer, and more committing than Mile High Club — generally excellent rock, with one notably polished, more run-out pitch (P3) and a long 55m opening pitch.
text.descent: Do not rappel Beyond Redlining itself — official route beta explicitly says it is equipped for emergency use but 'not recommended' as a descent line, since the angle and pitch lengths make it a poor rap line that would need two ropes or a 70m rope with awkward hangs. Instead, from the shared summit, descend via Mile High Club's dedicated rappel line, which works with a single 60m rope over 8 rappe

waypoints.name: Sunrise Mine Trailhead
waypoints.note: Sunrise Mine Trail #707 off Sunrise Mine Rd (FR 4065); approach to Vegan/Vega Tower group.
waypoints.directions: From Granite Falls, drive the Mountain Loop Highway east about 28 mi (about 17 mi past the Verlot Public Service Center) and turn right on Sunrise Mine Road (FS Road 4065). Follow this rough gravel road about 2.3 mi to its end at the Sunrise Mine Trailhead, at about 2,350 ft. High clearance is recommended, and a Northwest Forest Pass is required.

text.approach: Same Sunrise Mine Trail approach as Mile High Club and Beyond Redlining: follow the trail roughly 2.5 miles to the last major switchback at about 4,300 ft, then leave the trail for a cairned talus traverse heading northeast across two talus fields toward the Vega towers (shared with the other Vega North Tower routes). Where the traverse for Mile High Club and Beyond Redlining continues toward the base of the main west face, Marvin's Ear branches off into a gully to the right (east) of Vega North Tower. Follow this gully up through cedar and heather — vegetated, sometimes loose ground — to a notch on the skyline ridge. From the notch, the last bit to the pitch-one belay involves loose 3rd-class terrain with some exposed 4th-class moves, landing on a grassy ledge that serves as the first belay. Because this gully approach is steeper and more vegetated than the open talus used by Mile High Club, expect a slower, more route-finding-dependent final approach, and be cautious of loose blocks in the gully, especially with parties above.

text.overview: Marvin's Ear climbs the skyline ridge of Vega Tower — the sub-summit just east of Vega North Tower/Eros Tower — via a fully bolted 800-ft, 7-pitch alpine sport line (Grade III, 5.10b) through hard metaconglomerate rock. It was the first technical route up Vega Tower's west ridge proper (the only prior technical line, Starshot Ridge 5.8, was established in 1981 on a different aspect); climbing gets progressively more exposed as it skirts over the north face in the upper pitches.
text.descent: Marvin's Ear is rappelled back down its own line (not via Mile High Club). Bolted anchors are set roughly 30m apart along the route, so a single 60m rope will come up short in places — bring a 70m rope, which lets you link some of the 30m-spaced stations into longer raps and reduces the rappel count to roughly four full-length raps rather than seven pitch-by-pitch rappels. waypoints.directions: From Granite Falls, drive the Mountain Loop Highway east about 28 miles (17.1 miles past the Verlot Public Service Center) and turn right onto Sunrise Mine Road, FS Road 4065. Follow this rough gravel road about 2.2 miles to the trailhead at its end, near 2,350 ft; high clearance helps. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park.

text.approach: Start at the Cold Springs trailhead (about 5,600 ft) at the end of FR 8040 and walk the South Climb Trail up the old roadbed to its junction with the Round the Mountain Trail near 6,200 ft. Turn right (northwest) onto the Round the Mountain Trail and follow its up-and-down traverse for roughly two miles, much of it under snow in early season, to the stream draining the Avalanche Glacier basin near 6,100 ft. Follow the stream and the moraines above it to the moraine-filled bowl at about 7,200 ft, where the Avalanche Glacier route and the Southwest Chutes meet. The glacier begins above this bowl, and a camp here shortens the summit day.
text.overview: Approach via the PCT or the Shorthorn trail. Under normal conditions, climb the glacier on its right side. Parties go in late spring; expect mostly moderate to steep snow, sometimes with a headwall of alpine ice. Simul-climbing works for most of it, and pickets with a running belay give protection if needed. Descend by the south side or the neighboring snowfield.
text.descent: Climb out onto the summit plateau and head for the true summit, then descend the South Spur: cross the crater rim past Pikers Peak and follow the broad snow slopes of Crescent Ridge down to the Lunch Counter flats, where glissading is common on soft snow. From there the South Climb Trail runs down the old roadbed to Cold Springs, so no shuttle is needed if you started there. Going back down the Wh

text.approach: Start at the Killen Creek trailhead on FR 2329 north of Takhlakh Lake and follow Killen Creek Trail 113 south for about 3.2 miles through lodgepole forest and meadows to the Pacific Crest Trail junction near 6,100 ft. Cross the PCT onto the High Camp Trail, a rocky boot path that climbs a volcanic spur for about a mile to High Camp on a flat bench near 6,900 ft; the whole carry is roughly four miles and 2,300 ft. Camp here, since water comes only from snowmelt and the site is very exposed to wind. Above camp the trail ends and the way crosses moraines and old lava flows toward the north side of the mountain, so carry navigation for whiteouts. A Cascade Volcano Pass is required above 7,000 ft.

text.overview: A straightforward snow/ice line up the west face of Mount Adams's North Ridge, a more technical companion route to the standard North Ridge scramble.
text.descent: Descend the North Ridge, also called the North Cleaver, back toward High Camp. This is a walk-off over loose volcanic scree and boulders and is longer than it looks from above, with a real chance of knocking rock onto parties below, so spread out and move quickly through the worst sections. A rock band on the ridge can be downclimbed, and a short rope-assisted step is sometimes used by parties une

waypoints.name: Killen Creek Trailhead (Trail #113, FR-2329)
waypoints.directions: From Randle, drive south 1 mile on FR 25, bear left onto FR 23 and follow it about 32 miles to FR 2329, signed for Takhlakh Lake Campground. Turn onto FR 2329 and continue about 4.5 miles past Takhlakh Lake to the Killen Creek trailhead; from Trout Lake, FR 23 reaches the same FR 2329 junction in about 24 miles. A Northwest Forest Pass and a free self-issued wilderness permit are required.

text.approach: A free wilderness permit is self-issued at the trailhead. From the Riley Camp Trailhead, hike the Riley Camp Trail, staying off the Riley Cut-Off at the first junction, until it meets the Pacific Crest Trail. Turn south on the Pacific Crest Trail for a few minutes to Riley Creek and follow the creek up through boulders to the moraines at the foot of the Pinnacle Glacier. The headwall route begins at the base of the glacier.

text.overview: At the base the line may be obvious or not; several variations exist, so pick one. No cracks are on the route. The angle is mild at first and steep near the top. Rock bands seem stable, so objective danger looks modest. The route ends on the Pinnacle summit, an easy stroll from the main summit. Descend along the West Ridge; some parts are exposed though easy.

text.approach: Start at the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead (about 3,700 ft) at the end of Glacier Creek Road (FR 39) and follow Trail 677 through old growth, crossing several creeks that run higher in the afternoon than the morning. At about two miles and 4,700 ft you pass the former Kulshan Cabin site, then a signed junction: the left fork goes to the Coleman Glacier overlook and the right fork is the climbers' trail. Take the climbers' trail steeply up the Hogsback moraine ridge to the edge of the Coleman Glacier near 6,000 ft, where most parties camp. In winter and spring the road may be gated miles short of the trailhead, which adds distance, and the glacier is skinned from there toward the Deming.
text.descent: Ski or walk off by the way you came up. From the summit plateau drop down the Roman Wall, a snow slope of 35 to 45 degrees that is usually downclimbed or skied with care when it is icy, onto the Deming Glacier. Cross the saddle and ski the Coleman Glacier's upper slopes, picking a line through its crevasses and icefall; snow bridges sag in afternoon sun, and late season can force an end-run to cli

text.approach: Drive the Harts Pass road over the pass and down the Slate Creek road to the locked gate (about 3,800 ft). Walk the old South Fork Slate Creek road roughly a mile to the large bridge near 4,000 ft, then leave the road and travel south through open forest.
text.overview: The approach most climbers use: a bushwhack from the Slate Creek road to the east ridge, a steep vegetated slot, scrambling into the east cirque, then a ledge traverse to the summit gully on the west side of the top block.
text.descent: Retrace the route; descend the green slot carefully and keep to the forest on the left on the way down to avoid the alder.

text.approach: From the Buck Creek/Trinity Trailhead, hike roughly 6 miles through old burn/fireweed forest on the Buck Creek Trail, ford Buck Creek, then climb Mount Cleator's east ridge through logged forest. Contour left around 5,500 ft onto a boot path through an 'alder tunnel,' then traverse slippery heather and blueberry slopes to the base of twin gendarmes marking the start of the ridge. Gain the crest via a loose gully (easy to mid-5th class) right of the gendarmes.

text.overview: A striking, roughly 2,000 ft alpine granite ridge climb up Berge's east side - sustained low-to-mid 5th class rock broken by one 5.8 chimney crux - comparable in quality and length to the Complete North Ridge of Mount Stuart.
text.descent: Two descent options are documented. The recommended option reverses the approach back over the Berge-Cleator saddle - a ledge traverse above the lower slabs is key to avoiding elevation loss and regain - followed by brushy, wet alder and steep heather down to the boot path and trail. The alternative descends west via the High Pass trail, but adds distance and is best combined with also summiting B

text.approach: Drive the Mount Baker Highway (SR 542) east from Glacier about 12.5 miles and turn left onto the Hannegan Pass Road (FR 32), following it about 5 miles to the trailhead at its end; a Northwest Forest Pass is required to park. Hike the Hannegan Pass Trail about 4 miles to Hannegan Pass, drop into the Chilliwack River valley and cross the river, then climb onto Easy Ridge and follow its long, partly brushy climbers' path east. Cross the Imperfect Impasse, a moat-and-cliff notch that often needs a short low fifth-class downclimb, and climb snowfields to camp at Perfect Pass, roughly 16 miles and a full day from the car. From Perfect Pass, rope up, traverse around the Challenger Arm and cross about three miles of the crevassed Challenger Glacier to the base of the pinnacle. This is a genuine multi-day glacier expedition into one of the most remote, weather-exposed corners of the North Cascades, with essentially no bailout options once committed.

text.overview: East Face route on Poltergeist Pinnacle, the southernmost subsummit between Mount Challenger and Crooked Thumb in the Picket Range, approached via a glacier crossing to a dike-streaked granite shield. First climbed by Dan Aylward and Forrest Murphy, 2004.
text.descent: From the top of the technical climbing, simul-climb or belay short sections along the ridge crest (mostly low 5th class, up to 5.7) northward to Mount Challenger's main summit. From the true summit, descend the standard north-side Challenger Glacier route — the same line used for the peak's normal ascent — back down to Perfect Pass camp. waypoints.name: Hannegan Pass Trailhead
waypoints.note: From the end of the Hannegan Pass Road the route continues via Hannegan Pass, the Chilliwack valley, Easy Ridge and Perfect Pass (~6300 ft) before a multi-mile crossing of the Challenger Glacier to reach the pinnacle.
waypoints.directions: Drive the Mount Baker Highway (SR 542) east from Glacier about 12.5 miles, turn left onto the Hannegan Pass Road (FR 32) and follow it about 5 miles to the trailhead at its end, where a Northwest Forest Pass is required to park. That is the end of the driving. Come prepared for a genuine multi-day trip rather than a long day, since this is one of the most remote and weather-exposed corners of the North Cascades with essentially no bailout options once you are committed.

waypoints.name: Hannegan Pass
waypoints.note: Trail crests here; drop east on the trail past Boundary Camp into the Chilliwack River valley toward Easy Ridge.
waypoints.directions: Hike the Hannegan Pass Trail about 4 miles up the Ruth Creek valley, climbing steadily through forest and then open slopes to Hannegan Pass, where the trail crests.

waypoints.name: Boundary Camp
waypoints.note: Camp at the head of the Chilliwack River valley, just east of and below Hannegan Pass.
waypoints.directions: Drop east from the pass on the trail a little under a mile to Boundary Camp at the head of the Chilliwack River valley.

waypoints.name: Challenger Glacier Crossing
waypoints.note: Roped glacier travel across Challenger Glacier; crevasse hazard.
waypoints.directions: Continue down into the Chilliwack valley, cross the river, and climb onto Easy Ridge, following its long, partly brushy climbers' path east. Cross the Imperfect Impasse, a moat-and-cliff notch that often needs a short low fifth-class downclimb, climb snowfields to camp at Perfect Pass, then rope up and traverse east around the Challenger Arm onto the Challenger Glacier.

waypoints.name: Poltergeist Pinnacle
waypoints.directions: Continue roped across the upper glacier toward the cirque below the subsidiary summits, picking out the tower by the huge dark shield streaked with pale dikes at its base. The climb starts in a clean dihedral just left of the shield, about 20 ft above the bergschrund, and the East Face pitches lead to the top.

text.approach: Shares the same general approach drainage as the West Route (Jug Creek/Bluff Lake/Cliff Lake benches) to gain the west side of the mountain, then continues around/up to the base of the north ridge rather than the west-ridge saddle system.

text.overview: A roughly 1,500-ft alpine rock route up Chaval's north ridge: mostly moderate 3rd/4th-class scrambling on solid, well-fractured granitic rock, with two harder pitches on the steepest section near the top.
text.descent: Parties commonly traverse off the summit and descend the West Route's ramp/heather line rather than downclimbing the North Ridge.

text.overview: A direct, technical ridge line dropping northeast off Crowder's summit toward Pickell Pass. It is documented as a descent used by parties continuing a Pickets high-route traverse northward, not as a recommended way to reach Crowder's summit, and is significantly harder and more hazardous than the Southwest Route.
text.descent: From the summit, the ridge is down-climbed via a mix of loose, grassy Class 3-4 ledges with occasional low-5th-class moves, working around a large chasm partway down, and negotiating a final cliff band (found via a scree-slope break) before reaching Pickell Pass.

text.approach: Approach is up a brush-choked valley low in the Goodell Creek drainage — rough enough that even seasoned Cascades climbers have balked at it. This is the opposite (northeast) side of the peak from the standard Triumph Pass/Despair Lakes approach.
text.overview: A ~3,700 ft previously-unclimbed buttress line up Mt. Despair's northeast side to its north summit, opened in 2014: an easy 5.6 opening corner, a series of notches requiring short rappels, a stout 5.9 pitch through a deep summit-area cleft, a further steep pitch to the north ridge, and a snow-ridge finish.
text.descent: From the north summit, the first-ascent party exited over Triumph Pass and out the Thornton Lakes Trail rather than retracing the Goodell Creek approach.

text.approach: Drive State Route 20 to the Ross Dam trailhead between mileposts 134 and 135, 14.0 miles east of Newhalem (small lot, 4 standard plus 2 ADA spaces, no pass required). Hike the trail about a mile down to the Ross Lake water-taxi dock and take the Ross Lake Resort boat to Big Beaver Landing at about 1,600 ft (reserve in advance; parties report roughly $35 per person, and older reports quote a $50 minimum charge for a group). Without the boat, add a six-mile shoreline walk. From Big Beaver Landing follow the well-maintained Big Beaver Creek Trail about 10-11.5 miles through old-growth cedar past 39 Mile Camp to Luna Camp, then continue roughly 1 to 1.5 miles further north. Watch on the left for a small cairn or a scratched arrow on a split log marking the cut-off, and cross Big Beaver Creek on a log just north of where Access Creek enters it; some years you have to wade. Then bushwhack up Access Creek: wade the valley-bottom devil's club, cross to the north side and climb directly upslope through huckleberry, then several hours of heavy forest, deadfall and alternating slide alder. Near 3,800 ft cross back to the south bank where the brush pinches out between a tongue of forest and a tongue of talus, and follow cairns and a faint climbers' path up talus into Access Creek Basin at about 4,300 ft - a good first camp. text.overview: A more technical alternative to the standard glacier route, climbing directly up East Fury's east ridge over a subsidiary summit before joining the upper Fury Glacier to finish via the south ridge.
text.descent: There is no shortcut off East Fury - everything is a reversal. From the summit downclimb the 350 ft of Class 3 south ridge to the boulders, keeping off the steep summit snowfield, then traverse right below the cliff band back across the flat upper Fury Glacier at about 7,750 ft. text.approach: Park at the Necklace Valley (East Fork Foss) trailhead at the end of FR 68 and follow the East Fork Foss trail up the valley. The first five miles are gentle forest, gaining only about 600 ft, until a footlog crossing of the East Fork Foss River, then the trail climbs about 2,400 ft in three miles of steep, rooty switchbacks to Jade Lake and on up the Necklace Valley past the other lakes. Leave the valley trail at its upper end, where the hanging valley leads to La Bohn Lakes and the climb proper. Camps at the lakes or in Necklace Valley make this a two-day trip for most parties. From the end of the valley, climb the boulder gully or the waterfall route to La Bohn Gap (about 6,000 ft); the snow chute is the early-season option and needs an axe. The route starts from the gap, where a clear climbers' boot track turns north.
text.descent: Reverse the ridge and boot track to La Bohn Gap, downclimbing the class 2 to 3 rock, which is loose throughout. From the gap descend to the valley floor by the boulder gully, by the waterfall route beside it, or by the snow chute when it is soft; hard early-season snow calls for an axe and crampons. Then follow Necklace Valley trail past the lakes, down the steep 2,400 ft switchbacks to the footlo

text.approach: From the Necklace Valley Trailhead, follow the Necklace Valley Trail up the East Fork Foss River, over the river crossing and the steep climb beyond it, to the hanging valley holding La Bohn Lakes, where parties camp. From the lakes, climb the snow chute or talus to La Bohn Gap; the climb proper heads due north from the gap toward the summit.
